# Part 1: Importing data with R packages

## 1.1 - Female labour force participation (ILO)

### 1.1.1 - Explain which indicator you've chosen, and describe it briefly in words.

The ILOSTAT table of contents lists every series whose name contains "Labour force participation". The same rate is published in many versions, broken down by different characteristics. We narrow them down step by step.

```{r}
# Download the ILOSTAT table of contents for "Labour force participation"
toc <- get_ilostat_toc(search = "Labour force participation", quiet = TRUE)

# Number of matching series
nrow(toc)
names(toc)

# Identification of the different datasets, oldest start year first
toc |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  select(id, freq, data.start, data.end, n.ref_area) |>
  arrange(data.start) |>
  print()
```

Our research question is about long-run structural change, so we need annual data. Monthly or quarterly data would add seasonality we do not need.

```{r}
# Keep only annual series ("A" = annual)
annual <- toc |> filter(freq == "A")

# Number of candidates remaining
nrow(annual)

```

`r nrow(toc) - nrow(annual)` of the `r nrow(toc)` matching series are not annual and are dropped.

To keep women aged 45 to 54, the series must be split by both sex and age. Series split by sex and another characteristic (education, rural/urban area, marital status) but not by age only give one rate for all ages together, so they cannot be used.

```{r}
# Keep series with sex and age, oldest start year first
candidate <- annual |>
  filter(startsWith(id, "EAP_DWAP_SEX_AGE")) |>
  select(id, indicator.label, data.start, data.end, n.ref_area, n.records) |>
  arrange(data.start)


# Clean table with the dates
candidate |> select(id, data.start, data.end, n.ref_area) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Series", "First year", "Last year", "Countries and regions"))
```

```{r}
# Which candidate covers the most countries and regions? (desc() = largest first)
candidate |>
  select(id, n.ref_area) |>
  arrange(desc(n.ref_area))
```

We decided to choose the indicator EAP_DWAP_SEX_AGE_RT_A, "Labour force participation rate by sex and age (%)", in annual data. Seven annual series give the labour force participation rate with both sex and age as variable. However, only EAP_DWAP_SEX_AGE_RT_A ("Labour force participation rate by sex and age (%)") starts in 1946, which makes it the only series covering the whole period, from 1950 to 2025, that our research question needs.

Our indicator measures the share of the working-age population in a given sex and age group that is economically active (employed or looking for work). We are then able to select the share of women between 45 and 54 who are economically active.

We have chosen this indicator because:

- It has the longest time series and the most countries.
- It can be filtered for women in the right age bracket.
- The annual frequency best matches the research question (a long-run structural pattern: how female participation changes as countries develop). The extra detail of monthly or quarterly data would not be particularly relevant, and we do not need to deal with seasonality. For our research question, we need a sample that includes countries at different income levels.
- For the rest of the project, it allows us to merge it with GDP, which is also annual.

### 1.1.2 - Import the full series, i.e. all years available from 1950 to 2025.

Since we only need women aged 45 to 54, we use the filters so that the ILO server sends only the rows we need instead of the full dataset.

To filter by age, we need the exact code ILOSTAT uses for the 45 to 54 age group. We first check which age codes exist, using a small download (in our case Swiss women only) as an example.

```{r}
# Small test download: Switzerland, women only
test <- get_ilostat(
  id      = "EAP_DWAP_SEX_AGE_RT_A",   # our chosen dataset
  segment = "indicator",               # the dataset is organised by indicator
  filters = list(
    ref_area = "CHE",                  # only Switzerland, to keep it small
    sex      = "SEX_F"                 # only women
  ),
  quiet   = TRUE
)

# Show only the 10-year age bands
test |> distinct(classif1) |> filter(startsWith(classif1, "AGE_10YRBANDS"))
```

The ILO publishes the same data in several age-groups. The 10-year bands include the group we need, with the code `AGE_10YRBANDS_Y45-54`.

We can now download the full series for all countries, keeping only women aged 45 to 54 and the years 1950 to 2025.

```{r}
# Download the full series: all countries, women aged 45-54, 1950-2025
flfp_raw <- get_ilostat(
  id          = "EAP_DWAP_SEX_AGE_RT_A",
  segment     = "indicator",
  time_format = "num",                    # years as numbers, not text
  filters     = list(
    sex      = "SEX_F",                   # women
    classif1 = "AGE_10YRBANDS_Y45-54",    # age group 45-54 (code checked above)
    timefrom = 1950,                      # first year
    timeto   = 2025                       # last year
  ),
  quiet = TRUE
)

# Checks
distinct(flfp_raw, sex, classif1)   # should be one row: SEX_F, AGE_10YRBANDS_Y45-54
range(flfp_raw$time)                # first and last year
n_distinct(flfp_raw$ref_area)       # number of countries and regions
```

The filters worked: the data only contain women aged 45 to 54. The series covers `r min(flfp_raw$time)` to `r max(flfp_raw$time)` for `r n_distinct(flfp_raw$ref_area)` countries and territories. Please note that we keep the raw data here and that the cleaning (selecting variables, handling missing values, checking the country codes) is done in Part 3.

## 1.2 - GDP per capita (World Bank)

### 1.2.1 - Explain which indicator you've chosen, and describe it briefly in words.

The instruction mentioned two R packages that give access to the World Bank data API. Those are WDI and wbstats. In this project we are going to use the [WDI package](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/WDI/index.html). We choose the WDI package because it is the one that the instruction mentions in part 2 of the assignment but wbstats queries the same API and would give the same data.

We search for the indicators whose name contains "GDP per capita".

```{r}
# Search the World Bank indicators by name
search_wdi <- WDIsearch(string = "GDP per capita", field = "name") |> as.data.frame()
```

We filter for criteria (1) and (2), which can be read from the indicator name. The same currency makes countries comparable, and the inflation adjustment makes years comparable:

- Same currency: "US\$" or "international \$" (not "LCU" = local currency unit)
- Inflation-adjusted: "constant" prices, i.e. GDP measured every year at the prices of one base year (not "current" prices)

```{r}
# Flag the indicators that meet criteria (1) and (2)
candidates_W <- search_wdi |>
  mutate(
    same_currency = grepl("US\\$|international \\$", name),
    inflation_adj = grepl("constant", name, ignore.case = TRUE)
  )

candidates_W |> select(indicator, name, same_currency, inflation_adj)
```

Finally, we filter for criterion (3): we download the remaining candidates and compare their coverage, i.e. how far back each one goes and how many countries it covers.

```{r}
# Criteria (1) and (2): keep indicators with TRUE in both columns
finalists <- candidates_W |>
  filter(same_currency, inflation_adj) |>
  filter(indicator != "NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD.87")   # archived: no longer served by the API

df_finalists <- WDI(
  country   = "all",
  indicator = finalists$indicator,
  # start = 1960 could be added; however, World Bank data always start in 1960
  end       = 2025,
  extra     = TRUE   # adds "region", used to drop aggregates like "World"
)

# Criterion (3): compare how far back and how widely each finalist is covered
coverage <- df_finalists |>
  filter(region != "Aggregates") |> # keep countries only
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = any_of(finalists$indicator),
    names_to  = "indicator",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(value)) |>
  group_by(indicator) |>
  summarise(
    first_year  = min(year),           # earliest year with data
    last_year   = max(year),           # latest year with data
    n_countries = n_distinct(iso3c),   # number of countries
    n_obs       = n()                  # number of country-year values
  ) |>
  arrange(first_year)

coverage

# Store the two finalists' coverage (used in the text below)
kd  <- coverage |> filter(indicator == "NY.GDP.PCAP.KD")
ppp <- coverage |> filter(indicator == "NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD")
```

One finalist, NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD.87, is excluded: querying the World Bank API directly returns the message that the indicator was not found and may have been deleted or archived.

To conclude, we keep NY.GDP.PCAP.KD: it starts in `r kd$first_year` and covers `r kd$n_countries` countries, while NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD (in PPP, international \$) starts only in `r ppp$first_year` and covers `r ppp$n_countries` countries.

It measures the value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a year, divided by its population, in constant 2015 US dollars (adjusted for inflation, so that years can be compared).

### 1.2.2 - Import the full series, i.e. all years available up to 2025. What is the oldest date available?

Now that we have selected the indicator, we import the entire series from the earliest possible date.

```{r}
# Import GDP per capita (constant 2015 US$) for all countries, all years up to 2025
df_wb <- WDI(
  country   = "all",
  indicator = c(gdp_pc = "NY.GDP.PCAP.KD"),
  # start     = 1960 : the first date that is available
  end       = 2025,
  extra     = TRUE   # adds "region", used in Part 3 to drop aggregates like "World"
)

head(df_wb)
```

```{r}
# Oldest year with data
min(df_wb$year[!is.na(df_wb$gdp_pc)])
```

The oldest date available is `r min(df_wb$year[!is.na(df_wb$gdp_pc)])`.

# Part 2: Programming your own API functions

## 2.1 - Female labour force participation (ILO)

### 2.1.1 - Retrieve data using your own API wrapper

The URL starts with the base URL of the ILO server and the dataflow, which identifies the table we request (agency `ILO`, dataset `DF_EAP_DWAP_SEX_AGE_RT`, version `1.0`). It is followed by the key, with one slot per dimension separated by dots: country, frequency (`A` = annual), measure (left empty, so all values are returned), sex (`SEX_F`) and age band (`AGE_10YRBANDS_Y45-54`); an empty country slot returns all countries, and several countries can be joined with `+`. Finally, the query parameters `startPeriod` and `endPeriod` set the period, and `format=csvfilewithlabels` requests a CSV file that R can read directly.

```{r}
# define the function
get_ilodata <- function(country = "", year_from = 1950, year_to = 2025){

# Build the URL : base URL + dataflow (agency = ILO, dataset ID = DF_EAP_DWAP_SEX_AGE_RT, version = 1.0)
  base_url <- "https://sdmx.ilo.org/rest/data/ILO,DF_EAP_DWAP_SEX_AGE_RT,1.0/"

# Empty list to collect one data frame per country
  results <- list()

# Loop : repeat the request for each country of the vector
# with the default "" the loop runs once and returns all countries
  for (cty in country) {

# Creation of the key: one slot per dimension, separated by dots
# Format : country . frequency . measure (empty = all) . sex . age
    key <- paste0(cty, ".A..SEX_F.AGE_10YRBANDS_Y45-54")

# query parameters: start year, end year, output format
    final_url <- paste0(base_url,
                        key, "?startPeriod=",
                        year_from, "&endPeriod=",
                        year_to, "&dimensionAtObservation=AllDimensions",
                        "&format=csvfilewithlabels")
# dimensionAtObservation returns a flat table (one row per observation) and format ensures that we receive a CSV

# API call
# Create the request (nothing is sent yet)
    req <- request(final_url)

# httr2 stops by itself when the server answers with an error : we switch that off
# so that the answer always comes back and our own check below gives a clear error message
    req <- req_error(req, is_error = function(resp) FALSE)

# In case of issues with the server, we retry the request (and we pause at the end of each loop)
# If the server refuses temporarily (403) or is busy (429, 503), wait and try again (max 4 times)
# backoff : wait 5 seconds, then 10, then 15 before the next attempt
    req <- req_retry(req, max_tries = 4,
                     is_transient = function(resp) resp_status(resp) %in% c(403, 429, 503),
                     backoff = function(i) 5 * i)

# Send the request. If the server cannot be reached, show our own error message
    resp <- tryCatch(
      req_perform(req),
      error = function(e) {
        stop("Could not reach the ILO API. ",
             "URL: ", final_url, "\nOriginal error: ", conditionMessage(e))
      }
    )

# if request is not successful (anything other than 200 = OK)
    if (resp_status(resp) != 200){
      stop("The request was not successful for ", cty,
           " (HTTP ", resp_status(resp), "). URL: ", final_url)
    }

# Turn the CSV into a data frame with the columns we need
# and add it at the next free place of the list
    df <- read.csv(text = resp_body_string(resp))
    results[[length(results) + 1]] <- data.frame(
      ref_area  = df$REF_AREA,        # country code, "CHE"
      country   = df$Reference.area,  # country name
      time      = df$TIME_PERIOD,     # year
      obs_value = df$OBS_VALUE        # participation rate in %
    )

# Small pause between two countries, so that the server does not block us
    Sys.sleep(1)
  }

# Stack the data frames of all countries into one
  return(bind_rows(results))
}
```

### 2.1.2 - Test your API

#### 2.1.2.1 - Using a loop or a vectorized function, test your API. Apply your function to Switzerland, USA and Germany, filter the year to 2023 and check the output.

We apply our function to Switzerland, the USA and Germany for the year 2023. The loop is inside our function: it sends one request per country and stacks the results with `bind_rows()`.

```{r}
# Countries to test (ISO 3-letter codes used by the ILO)
countries <- c("CHE", "USA", "DEU")

# The loop is inside our function: one call is enough for the three countries
df_own <- get_ilodata(countries, year_from = 2023, year_to = 2023)

df_own

# Prepare our table for the comparison in 2.1.2.2 : keep the country code and the year
# (to match the rows with Rilostat) and rename our value to value_api (to tell it apart from Rilostat's)
df_own_short <- df_own |> select(ref_area, time, value_api = obs_value)

df_own_short

```
Our function returns 3 rows, one per country, all for the year 2023. Each row contains the ISO country code (`ref_area`), the country name, the year (`time`) and the labour force participation rate of women aged 45 to 54 in percent (`obs_value`). Switzerland has the highest rate (86.3 %), closely followed by Germany (85.8 %), while the rate in the USA is about 10 percentage points lower (76.5 %). All values lie between 0 and 100 and are plausible for this age group, so the function returns the data we requested.

#### 2.1.2.2 - Then do the same using the Rilostat package. Compare the results. Are the results the same?

We now do the same request with the `Rilostat` package and compare both results.

```{r}
# Same request with the Rilostat package : the three countries, women aged 45-54, year 2023
df_pkg <- get_ilostat(
  id = "EAP_DWAP_SEX_AGE_RT_A",          # same indicator as our function (A = annual)
  time_format = "num",                   # years as numbers, like in our function
  filters = list(
    ref_area = countries,                # CHE, USA, DEU (defined in 2.1.2.1)
    sex = "SEX_F",                       # women
    classif1 = "AGE_10YRBANDS_Y45-54",   # aged 45 to 54
    timefrom = 2023,
    timeto = 2023
  ),
  quiet = TRUE                           # no download messages in the report
)

# Put both results side by side (matched by country and year) and compute the difference
# value_pkg = Rilostat, value_api = our function, difference = 0 means identical
comparison <- df_pkg |>
  select(ref_area, time, value_pkg = obs_value) |>
  inner_join(df_own_short, by = c("ref_area", "time")) |>
  mutate(difference = value_api - value_pkg)

comparison
```

The results are the same. For Switzerland (86.278 %), Germany (85.836 %) and the USA (76.506 %) in 2023, our function and the Rilostat package return exactly the same participation rate: the difference is 0 for all three countries. Our API wrapper therefore retrieves the same data as the package.

We also compare the full series (all countries, 1950 to 2025) from our function with the Rilostat data imported in Part 1, and print only the rows where the two sources differ. This is the most complete test of our function, to make sure that our analysis is based on valid data.

```{r}
# Download the full series with our function (all countries, 1950-2025)
df_own_all <- get_ilodata()

# Put both sources side by side : Rilostat (Part 1) and our function
# full_join keeps every row, also the ones that exist in only one of the two sources
comparison_all <- flfp_raw |>
  select(ref_area, time, value_pkg = obs_value) |>
  full_join(df_own_all |> select(ref_area, time, value_api = obs_value),
            by = c("ref_area", "time")) |>
  mutate(difference = value_api - value_pkg)

# How many rows have which difference ? (0 = identical, 0.001 = rounding, NA = row in only one source)
comparison_all |> count(difference = round(difference, 3))

# Keep only the rows that are not identical :
# - a difference larger than 0.0011
# - or a missing value (the row exists in only one of the two sources)
# Why 0.0011 : the values are published with 3 decimals, and Rilostat (ILO bulk files) and our
# function (ILO SDMX API) round the same underlying value separately. Many rows therefore differ systematically by exactly 0.001 (e.g. 51.807 vs 51.808), which is a rounding gap, not a real difference.
# We use 0.0011 instead of 0.001 because the computer stores decimals with tiny errors
# (a gap of "0.001" can be stored as 0.0010000001 and would otherwise be counted as larger than 0.001)
different <- comparison_all |>
  filter(is.na(difference) | abs(difference) > 0.0011)

# Number of rows compared and number of rows that differ
nrow(comparison_all)
nrow(different)

# Print the rows that differ (empty table = both sources give the same data, up to rounding)
different
```

Our function returns exactly the same `r nrow(comparison_all)` country-year observations as Rilostat: no observation is missing in either source. `r sum(round(comparison_all$difference, 3) == 0, na.rm = TRUE)` values are identical, and the remaining `r sum(round(comparison_all$difference, 3) != 0, na.rm = TRUE)` differ by exactly 0.001 percentage points, always in the same direction. This is a rounding difference: the ILO publishes the rate with three decimals, and its bulk download files (used by Rilostat) and its SDMX API (used by our function) round the same underlying value separately. After allowing for this rounding, no difference remains, so our API wrapper retrieves the same data as the Rilostat package.

## 2.2 - Bonus: GDP per capita (World Bank)

### 2.2.1 - Import the data using your own API wrapper

The URL starts with the base URL of the World Bank API (version 2). The country and the indicator are then given as two path segments (`/country/CHE/indicator/NY.GDP.PCAP.KD`), and the query parameters set the output format (`format=json`, otherwise the API returns XML), the period (`date=1960:2025`) and the number of rows per page (`per_page=20000`, high enough to receive all observations in one page). The answer is a JSON list: its first element contains the metadata (for example the total number of observations) and its second element contains the observations.

```{r}
# define the function
get_wbdata <- function(indicator = "NY.GDP.PCAP.KD", country = "all", year_from = 1960, year_to = 2025){

# Base URL of the World Bank API (version 2)
  base_url <- "https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/"

# Empty list to collect one data frame per country
  results <- list()

# Loop : repeat the request for each country of the vector
# with the default "all" the loop runs once and returns all countries and regions
  for (cty in country) {

# Build the URL : base URL + country + indicator (path parameters) + query parameters
# format=json : otherwise the API returns XML
# date=START:END : the period
# per_page=20000 : number of rows per page, high enough to receive everything in one page
    final_url <- paste0(base_url, cty,
                        "/indicator/", indicator,
                        "?format=json",
                        "&date=", year_from, ":", year_to,
                        "&per_page=20000")

# API call
# Create the request (nothing is sent yet)
    req <- request(final_url)

# httr2 stops by itself when the server answers with an error : we switch that off
# so that the answer always comes back and our own check below gives a clear error message
    req <- req_error(req, is_error = function(resp) FALSE)

# In case of issues with the server, we retry the request (and we pause at the end of each loop)
# If the server refuses temporarily (403) or is busy (429, 503), wait and try again (max 4 times)
# backoff : wait 5 seconds, then 10, then 15 before the next attempt
    req <- req_retry(req, max_tries = 4,
                     is_transient = function(resp) resp_status(resp) %in% c(403, 429, 503),
                     backoff = function(i) 5 * i)

# Send the request. If the server cannot be reached, show our own error message
    resp <- tryCatch(
      req_perform(req),
      error = function(e) {
        stop("Could not reach the World Bank API. ", "URL: ", final_url, "\nOriginal error: ", conditionMessage(e))
      }
    )

# if request is not successful (anything other than 200 = OK)
    if (resp_status(resp) != 200){
      stop("The request was not successful for ", cty, " (HTTP ", resp_status(resp), "). URL: ", final_url)
    }

# Turn the JSON answer into an R list
# first element = metadata (page, total number of observations), second element = the observations
    body <- resp_body_json(resp)

# An invalid indicator still returns status 200, with a message instead of data
    if (!is.null(body[[1]]$message)) {
      stop("World Bank API error for ", cty, ": ", body[[1]]$message[[1]]$value, ". URL: ", final_url)
    }

    meta <- body[[1]]
    obs  <- body[[2]]

# No observations at all (e.g. no data for this country and period)
    if (is.null(obs) || length(obs) == 0) {
      stop("No data returned for ", cty, ". URL: ", final_url)
    }

# Turn the list of observations into a data frame (one row per observation)
# sapply goes through each observation and extracts one field ; missing values (NULL) become NA
    df <- data.frame(
      country   = sapply(obs, function(x) x$country$value),   # country name
      iso2c     = sapply(obs, function(x) x$country$id),       # 2-letter code (also exists for regions)
      iso3c     = sapply(obs, function(x) x$countryiso3code),  # 3-letter code (empty for some regions)
      year      = as.integer(sapply(obs, function(x) x$date)), # year
      indicator = sapply(obs, function(x) x$indicator$id),     # indicator code
      value     = sapply(obs, function(x) if (is.null(x$value)) NA else x$value)  # GDP per capita
    )

# Check that we received all the observations the API says exist (first element of the answer)
    if (nrow(df) != meta$total) {
      warning("Received ", nrow(df), " of ", meta$total,
              " observations for ", cty, ". Increase per_page.")
    }

# Add the data frame at the next free place of the list
    results[[length(results) + 1]] <- df

# Small pause between two countries, so that the server does not block us
    Sys.sleep(1)
  }

# Stack the data frames of all countries into one
  return(bind_rows(results))
}
```

### 2.2.2 - Test your API

#### 2.2.2.1 - Using a loop or a vectorized function, test your API. Apply your function to Switzerland, USA and Germany, filter the year to 2023 and check the output.

We apply our function to Switzerland, the USA and Germany for the year 2023. As for the ILO, the loop is inside our function: it sends one request per country and stacks the results with `bind_rows()`.

```{r}
# Countries to test (ISO 3-letter codes, accepted by the World Bank API)
countries_wb <- c("CHE", "USA", "DEU")

# The loop is inside our function: one call is enough for the three countries
df_wb_own <- get_wbdata("NY.GDP.PCAP.KD", countries_wb, year_from = 2023, year_to = 2023)

df_wb_own
```

Our function returns 3 rows, one per country, all for the year 2023. Each row contains the country name, the 2-letter code (`iso2c`), the 3-letter code (`iso3c`), the year, the indicator (`NY.GDP.PCAP.KD`) and its value: GDP per capita in constant 2015 US dollars. In 2023, Switzerland has the highest GDP per capita (about 92,948 US$), ahead of the USA (about 65,667 US$) and Germany (about 44,369 US$). The values are positive and plausible for three high-income economies, so the function returns the data we requested.

#### 2.2.2.2 - Then do the same using the WDI package. Are the results the same?

We now do the same request with the `WDI` package and compare both results.

```{r}
# Same request with the WDI package : the three countries, year 2023
df_wb_pkg <- WDI(
  country = c("CH", "US", "DE"),          # WDI uses the 2-letter codes
  indicator = "NY.GDP.PCAP.KD",           # GDP per capita, constant 2015 US$
  start = 2023,
  end = 2023
)

# Put both results side by side (matched by country and year) and compute the difference
# value_pkg = WDI, value_api = our function, difference = 0 means identical
comparison_wb <- df_wb_pkg |>
  select(iso3c, year, value_pkg = NY.GDP.PCAP.KD) |>
  inner_join(
    df_wb_own |> select(iso3c, year, value_api = value),
    by = c("iso3c", "year")
  ) |>
  mutate(difference = value_api - value_pkg)

comparison_wb
```

The results are the same. For Switzerland (about 92,948 US$), Germany (about 44,369 US$) and the USA (about 65,667 US$) in 2023, our function and the WDI package return exactly the same GDP per capita: the difference is 0 for all three countries. This is expected, since both query the same World Bank API.

As for the ILO, we go further and compare the full series (all countries and regions, 1960 to 2025) from our function with the WDI data imported in Part 1, and print only the rows where the two sources differ.

```{r}
# Download the full series with our function (all countries and regions, 1960-2025)
df_wb_own_all <- get_wbdata("NY.GDP.PCAP.KD")

# Prepare both sources : same columns, with a different name for the value
# We match the rows with iso2c (2-letter code) and year : unlike iso3c, iso2c also exists for regions
wb_pkg_all <- df_wb |> select(iso2c, year, value_pkg = gdp_pc)
wb_api_all <- df_wb_own_all |> select(iso2c, year, value_api = value)

# Rows that exist in only one of the two sources (0 and 0 = both sources have the same rows)
nrow(anti_join(wb_pkg_all, wb_api_all, by = c("iso2c", "year")))
nrow(anti_join(wb_api_all, wb_pkg_all, by = c("iso2c", "year")))

# Put both sources side by side and compute the difference
comparison_wb_all <- inner_join(wb_pkg_all, wb_api_all, by = c("iso2c", "year")) |>
  mutate(difference = value_api - value_pkg)

# Keep only the rows that are not identical :
# - a value that is missing (NA) in one source but not in the other
# - or a real difference between the two values
# Unlike the ILO data, the World Bank data has many NA values (one row for every year),
# so two NA values count as identical here.
# Both sources query the same World Bank API, so we expect no rounding gap :
# 0.000001 only ignores the tiny errors with which the computer stores decimals
different_wb <- comparison_wb_all |>
  filter(is.na(value_api) != is.na(value_pkg) |
           (!is.na(difference) & abs(difference) > 0.000001))

# Number of rows compared and number of rows that differ
nrow(comparison_wb_all)
nrow(different_wb)

# Print the rows that differ (empty table = both sources give exactly the same data)
different_wb
```

Both sources contain exactly the same `r nrow(comparison_wb_all)` rows (266 countries and regions × 66 years, from 1960 to 2025): no row exists in only one of them. All values are identical, and the missing values (`NA`) are in the same places in both sources, so not a single row differs. Unlike for the ILO, there is not even a rounding gap, because our function and the WDI package query the same World Bank API. Our API wrapper therefore retrieves exactly the same data as the WDI package.

# Part 3: Cleaning, merging and analysing the data

We use the data imported with the R packages in Part 1. Part 2 showed that our own API functions return the same values (up to rounding at the third decimal place for the ILO), and the package data also contains the variables we need for the cleaning and the analysis, such as the region and the income group of each country.

```{r}
# Import the data saved in Part 1 (Rilostat and WDI)
df_ilo <- readRDS("data/df_ilostat_womenparticipation.RDS")
df_wb  <- readRDS("data/df_WorldBank_gdp_capita.RDS")

# Small helper for the text : write large numbers with a thousands separator (17556 -> 17,556)
fmt <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",")
```

## 3.1 - First data exploration

### 3.1.1 - Comment on the structure of your data frames and describe the types of variables they contain.

In order to comment on the structure of the data frames, we first get a summary of the data with the `glimpse` function:

```{r}
# Overview of each data frame : number of rows and columns, type and first values of each variable
glimpse(df_ilo)
glimpse(df_wb)
```

Both data frames have one row per area and year. `df_ilo` has `r fmt(nrow(df_ilo))` rows from `r min(df_ilo$time)` to `r max(df_ilo$time)`, and `df_wb` has `r fmt(nrow(df_wb))` rows from `r min(df_wb$year)` to `r max(df_wb$year)`.

`df_ilo` has `r sum(sapply(df_ilo, is.numeric))` numeric and `r sum(sapply(df_ilo, is.character))` character columns, and `df_wb` has `r sum(sapply(df_wb, is.numeric))` numeric and `r sum(sapply(df_wb, is.character))` character columns. In `df_ilo`, the numeric columns are `time` (the year) and `obs_value`, both stored as doubles, and `obs_value` is the participation rate of women aged 45 to 54 in percent. In `df_wb`, they are `year` (the year) and `gdp_pc`, and `gdp_pc` is GDP per capita in constant 2015 US dollars.

### 3.1.2 - Load the datasets. Briefly describe the content of each dataset according to the five key aspects described above. For aspect 3 (quality), perform two smell tests per dataset.

Both datasets were loaded at the start of Part 3 with `readRDS()`.

#### df_ilo

**1. Definitions.** `obs_value` is the labour force participation rate, the share of women aged 45 to 54 who are either employed or looking for work. `ref_area` is the country code and `time` is the year.

**2. Units.** `obs_value` is in percent, and `time` is in calendar years.

**3. Quality.** We chose these two tests because they check what matters most for the later analysis. Duplicate country-years would be counted twice after the merge, and a participation rate is a percentage, so missing or out-of-range values would point to errors in the data.

```{r}
# Smell test 1: duplicate country-year rows (each country should appear only once per year)
dup_ilo <- df_ilo |>
  count(ref_area, time) |>
  filter(n > 1)

nrow(dup_ilo)

# Smell test 2: missing values and range of the rate (a percentage must lie between 0 and 100)
sum(is.na(df_ilo$obs_value))
range(df_ilo$obs_value)
```

`r nrow(dup_ilo)` country-years appear more than once, so there are no duplicates. There are `r sum(is.na(df_ilo$obs_value))` missing values, and the values run from `r min(df_ilo$obs_value)` to `r max(df_ilo$obs_value)`, which is plausible for a percentage. A maximum of exactly 100 is surprising for women aged 45 to 54, so we look at it in section 3.2.1.

**4. Unit of observation.** Each row is one country or area in one year. There are `r n_distinct(df_ilo$ref_area)` codes, but only 193 UN member states, so we investigate this further in section 3.2.1.

**5. Time structure.** It is an unbalanced panel from `r min(df_ilo$time)` to `r max(df_ilo$time)`. Coverage is uneven, with far more observations in recent years than in early decades.

#### df_wb

**1. Definitions.** `gdp_pc` is GDP per capita, the value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a year divided by its population. It is adjusted for inflation. `iso3c` is the 3-letter country code and `year` is the year. `income` is the World Bank income group classification of a country.

**2. Units.** `gdp_pc` is in constant 2015 US dollars, and `year` is in calendar years.

**3. Quality.** We chose these two smell tests because they check what matters most for the merge. Groups of countries are not countries and would be counted as extra observations, and rows without a country code cannot be matched to the ILO data.

```{r}
# Smell test 1: using regions, we count the areas that are groups of countries, not countries
n_groups_wb <- df_wb |>
  distinct(country, region) |>
  filter(is.na(region) | region == "Aggregates") |>
  nrow()

n_groups_wb

# Smell test 2: rows with an empty country code (they cannot be matched to the ILO data)
sum(df_wb$iso3c == "")
```

`r n_groups_wb` of the `r n_distinct(df_wb$country)` areas are aggregates or groups, such as "World" or "High income", and not countries. `iso3c` is also empty for `r sum(df_wb$iso3c == "")` rows (`r n_distinct(df_wb$country[df_wb$iso3c == ""])` areas), so these rows cannot be matched to the ILO codes.

**4. Unit of observation.** Each row is one area in one year. Of the `r n_distinct(df_wb$country)` areas, `r n_distinct(df_wb$country) - n_groups_wb` are countries or territories, and `r n_groups_wb` are groups of countries.

**5. Time structure.** It is a panel from `r min(df_wb$year)` to `r max(df_wb$year)`. Every area has a row for every year (`r n_distinct(df_wb$country)` × `r n_distinct(df_wb$year)` = `r fmt(nrow(df_wb))` rows), so any missing values appear as `NA`, not as absent rows.

## 3.2 - Data cleaning

### 3.2.1 - ILO data (`df_ilo`)

`ref_area` identifies the countries, so we keep it. However, there are `r n_distinct(df_ilo$ref_area)` codes and only 193 UN member states, so we investigate the extra codes. We compare our codes with the list of UN member states from the `memberstates` package, and use the `countrycode` package to add the country names.

```{r}
# memberstates$un is a list of the 5 UN regional groups : we take the codes of each group, put them together, and remove the duplicate (note that it only removes turkey once)
un_members <- memberstates$un |>
  lapply(function(group) group$iso3c) |>
  unlist() |>
  unique()

# Check : the list must contain the 193 UN member states (the render stops otherwise (avoid stupid 194 countries from before))
length(un_members)
stopifnot(length(un_members) == 193)

# One row per code of our ILO data : number of observations, period covered and country name
# custom_match : codes used by the ILO that countrycode does not know
ilo_codes <- df_ilo |>
  group_by(ref_area) |>
  summarise(n_obs      = n(),
            first_year = min(time),
            last_year  = max(time)) |>
  mutate(name = countrycode(ref_area, origin = "iso3c", destination = "country.name",
                            custom_match = c(KOS = "Kosovo", ANT = "Netherlands Antilles")))

# Codes that are not UN member states, sorted by name
not_un <- ilo_codes |>
  filter(!ref_area %in% un_members) |>
  arrange(name)

nrow(not_un)
not_un |> print(n = Inf)

# Does the World Bank have data for ANT ? (0 = no, it would be lost in the merge anyway)
sum(df_wb$iso3c == "ANT")
```

`r nrow(not_un)` codes are not UN member states: 1 no longer exists (ANT), 3 are disputed or partly recognised (KOS, TWN, PSE) and the rest are territories of other countries. We only delete ANT, the one code of a country that no longer exists. The Netherlands Antilles were dissolved in 2010, and the World Bank has no data for them, so they could not be used in the merged data anyway.The other codes are separate areas with their own data, and dropping them would remove observations without a clear reason. We keep in mind that they are not all sovereign countries when we interpret the results.

```{r}
# Manual decision, after reading the list above : ANT (Netherlands Antilles) no longer exists
codes_to_drop <- c("ANT")

df_ilo_clean <- df_ilo |>
  filter(!ref_area %in% codes_to_drop)

# The render stops if a dropped code is still in the data
stopifnot(!any(codes_to_drop %in% df_ilo_clean$ref_area))

# Check : number of codes before and after, and number of observations removed
n_distinct(df_ilo$ref_area)
n_distinct(df_ilo_clean$ref_area)
nrow(df_ilo) - nrow(df_ilo_clean)
```

`source` could explain duplicate country-year rows, but as seen in the smell test from 3.1.2, there are no duplicates. The column is therefore not needed.

```{r}
# source is only removed because there are no duplicate country-years (smell test 1 in 3.1.2)
stopifnot(nrow(dup_ilo) == 0)

# Remove the source column (no duplicates to explain)
df_ilo_clean <- df_ilo_clean |>
  select(-source)
```

We must then look at the `indicator`, `sex` and `classif1` categories to see whether they represent only one value (for `sex` it must be female and for `classif1` it must be women between the age of 45 and 54).

```{r}
# Each column should contain only one value (our indicator, women, aged 45-54)
distinct(df_ilo, indicator)
distinct(df_ilo, sex)
distinct(df_ilo, classif1)

# The render stops if one of these columns contains more than one value
stopifnot(n_distinct(df_ilo$indicator) == 1,
          n_distinct(df_ilo$sex) == 1,
          n_distinct(df_ilo$classif1) == 1)
```

Each has one value: women, aged 45 to 54. Therefore, these columns are no longer needed.

```{r}
# Remove the columns with only one value
df_ilo_clean <- df_ilo_clean |>
  select(-indicator, -sex, -classif1)
```

We now take a look at the metadata columns `obs_status`, `note_classif`, `note_indicator` and `note_source`. These are codes we cannot interpret and are not needed for the analysis, and three of them are almost entirely empty. Hence we can delete them too.

```{r}
# Remove the metadata columns (codes and notes not needed for the analysis)
df_ilo_clean <- df_ilo_clean |>
  select(-obs_status, -note_classif, -note_indicator, -note_source)
```

We check that the columns were deleted accurately and comment on `time` and `obs_value`.

```{r}
# Only our three variables are left, without missing values (the render stops otherwise)
stopifnot(setequal(names(df_ilo_clean), c("ref_area", "time", "obs_value")),
          !anyNA(df_ilo_clean))

# Check of the remaining columns : type, missing values and distribution
skim(df_ilo_clean)
```

We can see that `n_missing` is zero for both columns, which indicates there are no NA values (as already seen for `obs_value` in 3.1.2). `time` is numeric (years) with a minimum of `r min(df_ilo_clean$time)` and a maximum of `r max(df_ilo_clean$time)`. The mean of `time` is nearer to `r max(df_ilo_clean$time)` than `r min(df_ilo_clean$time)` because there are more datapoints, and hence more rows with a value, the closer we get to today.

```{r}
# Summary of our variable of interest : the participation rate
summary(df_ilo_clean$obs_value)
```

`obs_value` is the participation rate in percent. The summary shows a minimum of `r round(min(df_ilo_clean$obs_value), 3)`, a median of `r round(median(df_ilo_clean$obs_value), 3)`, a mean of `r round(mean(df_ilo_clean$obs_value), 3)` and a maximum of `r round(max(df_ilo_clean$obs_value), 3)`. All values lie between 0 and 100, which is plausible for a percentage (see 3.1.2). The mean is below the median, so some countries with very low participation pull the average down. A maximum of exactly 100 is surprising for women aged 45 to 54, so we check it below.

```{r}
# Which areas have a participation rate of exactly 100 % ?
full_rate <- df_ilo_clean |>
  filter(obs_value == 100)

full_rate |> print(n = Inf)
```

The only area with a rate of exactly 100 % is `r paste(unique(full_rate$ref_area), collapse = ", ")`. As MSR (Montserrat) is a very small territory, this result, although improbable, is plausible, and therefore we keep it in our data.

In summary, we keep only `ref_area`, `time` and `obs_value`. `ref_area` (country code) and `time` (year) identify each observation and will be used to merge with the World Bank data, and `obs_value` (participation rate in %) is our variable of interest.

### 3.2.2 - World Bank data (`df_wb`)

`country` identifies the areas, so we keep it. There are `r n_distinct(df_wb$country)` of them, so we must make sure we only keep countries and no groups. As seen in 3.1.2, `r n_groups_wb` of the `r n_distinct(df_wb$country)` areas are aggregates or groups (such as "World" or "High income") and not countries. We use the `region` column to remove them, as they either have the region "Aggregates" or no region at all.

```{r}
# Remove the groups of countries : region "Aggregates" or no region at all
df_wb_clean <- df_wb |>
  filter(!is.na(region), region != "Aggregates")

# Check : only real regions should remain (the render stops if an aggregate is left)
count(df_wb_clean, region)
stopifnot(!any(df_wb_clean$region == "Aggregates"))
```

The count shows that no aggregates or missing regions remain. As seen in 3.1.2, `iso3c` is also empty for some rows. These cannot be matched to the ILO data, so we remove any that are left.

```{r}
# Remove the rows without a 3-letter country code (they cannot be merged)
df_wb_clean <- df_wb_clean |>
  filter(iso3c != "")

# The render stops if an empty or missing country code is left
stopifnot(all(df_wb_clean$iso3c != ""), !anyNA(df_wb_clean$iso3c))
```

We keep `iso3c` and delete `iso2c`, because `iso3c` is the 3-letter code that is also used in `df_ilo`. `status` is empty in every row, and `lastupdated` is the date the website was last updated, which is irrelevant to our analysis. We have now used `region` to clean the list of countries, so we have no further use for it. `capital`, `longitude`, `latitude` and `lending` are not relevant to our analysis either. We keep `income`, as it is needed in section 3.4.2 to compare rich and poor countries.

```{r}
# Remove the columns not needed for the analysis
df_wb_clean <- df_wb_clean |>
  select(-iso2c, -status, -lastupdated, -region,
         -capital, -longitude, -latitude, -lending)

# Only the variables we need are left (the render stops otherwise)
stopifnot(setequal(names(df_wb_clean), c("country", "iso3c", "year", "gdp_pc", "income")))

# Check that the columns were properly deleted
skim(df_wb_clean)
```

We check that the cleaned data is complete and as expected, because missing country codes cannot be merged, and the number of areas, the years and the income groups should match what we kept.

```{r}
# Empty or missing country codes
sum(df_wb_clean$iso3c == "")
sum(is.na(df_wb_clean$iso3c))

# Size : number of areas (all areas minus the groups found in 3.1.2) and number of rows
n_distinct(df_wb_clean$country)
nrow(df_wb_clean)

# Type and range of year
class(df_wb_clean$year)
range(df_wb_clean$year)

# Missing GDP values
sum(is.na(df_wb_clean$gdp_pc))

# Income groups
count(df_wb_clean, income)
```

Most checks show no problems: there are no empty or missing country codes, the data has the expected `r n_distinct(df_wb_clean$country)` areas and `r fmt(nrow(df_wb_clean))` rows, `year` is numeric and runs from `r min(df_wb_clean$year)` to `r max(df_wb_clean$year)`, and every area has an income group. The only issue is the `r fmt(sum(is.na(df_wb_clean$gdp_pc)))` NA values in `gdp_pc`, which must be understood and dealt with.

```{r}
# Missing GDP values by year
df_wb_clean |>
  filter(is.na(gdp_pc)) |>
  count(year)

# Countries with the most missing values
df_wb_clean |>
  filter(is.na(gdp_pc)) |>
  count(country, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(50)
```

These NA values make the panel unbalanced. By year, they are concentrated in the early decades and fall steadily towards today. By country, a few small territories have no GDP at all, and others are missing many years. A missing `gdp_pc` carries no information and cannot be used in the analysis, so we drop those rows. This leaves `r fmt(sum(!is.na(df_wb_clean$gdp_pc)))` observations.

```{r}
# Number of rows before removing the NA values
nrow(df_wb_clean)

# Remove the rows without GDP per capita
df_wb_clean <- df_wb_clean |>
  filter(!is.na(gdp_pc))

# Check that the NA values were taken out of the data frame (the render stops otherwise)
sum(is.na(df_wb_clean$gdp_pc))
stopifnot(!anyNA(df_wb_clean$gdp_pc))
```

We now move on to `gdp_pc`. As it is already in 2015 US Dollars, there is no adjustment needed. However, we also need it in logs, so we add the log of `gdp_pc` as a new variable.

```{r}
# As log(0) is undefined, we must check that no GDP value is 0 or negative (the render stops otherwise)
any(df_wb_clean$gdp_pc <= 0)
stopifnot(all(df_wb_clean$gdp_pc > 0))

# Add the log of GDP per capita
df_wb_clean <- df_wb_clean |>
  mutate(log_gdp_pc = log(gdp_pc))
```

```{r}
# Summary of our variables of interest : GDP per capita and its log
summary(df_wb_clean$gdp_pc)
summary(df_wb_clean$log_gdp_pc)
```

`gdp_pc` ranges from about `r fmt(round(min(df_wb_clean$gdp_pc)))` to `r fmt(round(max(df_wb_clean$gdp_pc)))` US dollars, and its mean (`r fmt(round(mean(df_wb_clean$gdp_pc)))`) is far above the median (`r fmt(round(median(df_wb_clean$gdp_pc)))`), so a few very rich economies pull the average up. After taking logs, the mean (`r round(mean(df_wb_clean$log_gdp_pc), 2)`) is close to the median (`r round(median(df_wb_clean$log_gdp_pc), 2)`), so the distribution is much more symmetric. There are no zero or negative values.

```{r}
# Final check of the cleaned World Bank data
skim(df_wb_clean)
```

We keep `country` and `iso3c` to identify each area (`iso3c` is the 3-letter code also used in `df_ilo` and will be used for the merge), `year` to identify the period, `gdp_pc` and `log_gdp_pc` as our variables of interest and `income` because it is needed in section 3.4.2.

We save the cleaned data, as in Part 1, so that the next sections can start from these files.

```{r}
# Save the cleaned data (R format)
saveRDS(df_ilo_clean, "data/df_ilo_clean.RDS")
saveRDS(df_wb_clean,  "data/df_wb_clean.RDS")
```

## 3.3 - Merge the data

### 3.3.1 - Which variable(s) will you use to perform the merge?

We merge on two keys together: the country code (`ref_area` in the ILO data, `iso3c` in the World Bank data) and the year (`time`, `year`). The unit of observation is the country-year in both, so the merge is one-to-one; the code alone would match every year with every year (many-to-many). We use codes because the sources spell names differently.

### 3.3.2 - Are there any additional cleaning steps required before merging the datasets, if any?

Yes: the keys need the same names, types and values, and must be unique.

```{r}
# Type of the year column in each dataset
class(df_ilo_clean$time)
class(df_wb_clean$year)

# Same key names and types : rename the ILO columns, year as integer
df_ilo_merge <- df_ilo_clean |>
  select(iso3c = ref_area, year = time, flfp = obs_value) |>
  mutate(year = as.integer(year))

# Keep only the keys and GDP (name and income group are added after the merge)
df_wb_merge <- df_wb_clean |>
  select(iso3c, year, gdp_pc, log_gdp_pc)

# Check : duplicated country-years in each dataset (0 = none)
df_ilo_merge |>
  count(iso3c, year) |>
  filter(n > 1) |>
  nrow()
df_wb_merge |>
  count(iso3c, year) |>
  filter(n > 1) |>
  nrow()
```

`time` is `r class(df_ilo_clean$time)` and `year` `r class(df_wb_clean$year)`: we rename the ILO keys and make years integers. No key is duplicated.

```{r}
# Names for the codes that countrycode does not know
custom_names <- c(KOS = "Kosovo", XKX = "Kosovo", CHI = "Channel Islands")

# ILO codes without a match in the World Bank data
df_ilo_merge |>
  distinct(iso3c) |>
  anti_join(distinct(df_wb_merge, iso3c), by = "iso3c") |>
  mutate(name = countrycode(iso3c, "iso3c", "country.name",
                            custom_match = custom_names))

# World Bank codes without a match in the ILO data
df_wb_merge |>
  distinct(iso3c) |>
  anti_join(distinct(df_ilo_merge, iso3c), by = "iso3c") |>
  mutate(name = countrycode(iso3c, "iso3c", "country.name",
                            custom_match = custom_names))
```

Kosovo has two codes (KOS, XKX), so we recode the ILO one.

```{r}
# Recode Kosovo to the World Bank code
df_ilo_merge <- df_ilo_merge |>
  mutate(iso3c = if_else(iso3c == "KOS", "XKX", iso3c))

# Check : codes still without a match in each direction
ilo_only <- df_ilo_merge |>
  distinct(iso3c) |>
  anti_join(distinct(df_wb_merge, iso3c), by = "iso3c")
wb_only <- df_wb_merge |>
  distinct(iso3c) |>
  anti_join(distinct(df_ilo_merge, iso3c), by = "iso3c")

nrow(ilo_only)
nrow(wb_only)
```

Now only `r nrow(ilo_only)` ILO and `r nrow(wb_only)` World Bank codes are unmatched. Periods: ILO `r min(df_ilo_merge$year)`–`r max(df_ilo_merge$year)`, World Bank `r min(df_wb_merge$year)`–`r max(df_wb_merge$year)`.

### 3.3.3 - What type of merge is appropriate (e.g., right join, left join, full join, etc.) in this case?

```{r}
# The four joins on the same keys : rows, countries, rows with both values
df_joins <- bind_rows(
  inner = inner_join(df_ilo_merge, df_wb_merge, by = c("iso3c", "year")),
  left  = left_join(df_ilo_merge, df_wb_merge, by = c("iso3c", "year")),
  right = right_join(df_ilo_merge, df_wb_merge, by = c("iso3c", "year")),
  full  = full_join(df_ilo_merge, df_wb_merge, by = c("iso3c", "year")),
  .id = "join"
) |>
  group_by(join) |>
  summarise(rows      = n(),
            countries = n_distinct(iso3c),
            both      = sum(!is.na(flfp) & !is.na(gdp_pc)))

knitr::kable(df_joins, col.names = c("Join (x = ILO, y = World Bank)", "Rows",
                                     "Countries", "Rows with both values"))

# Master panel : full join
df_merged <- full_join(df_ilo_merge, df_wb_merge, by = c("iso3c", "year"))
```

We use a full join: 3.4.1 needs participation alone, 3.4.2 GDP alone and 3.5 both, and only the full join keeps all `r df_joins$countries[df_joins$join == "full"]` countries. An inner join would drop `r nrow(df_ilo_merge) - df_joins$rows[df_joins$join == "inner"]` participation rows, including all `r sum(df_ilo_merge$year < min(df_wb_merge$year))` before `r min(df_wb_merge$year)`. A left join on the ILO data would drop `r fmt(nrow(df_wb_merge) - df_joins$rows[df_joins$join == "inner"])` GDP rows and bias the GDP trends.

### 3.3.4 - What are the implications of your choice of merging method for your analysis?

```{r}
# Countries with both values in the years compared in 3.5.3
df_merged |>
  filter(!is.na(flfp), !is.na(gdp_pc), year %in% c(1970, 1990, 2010, 2020)) |>
  count(year)
```

The full join turns the rows missing from one source into explicit `NA`s: `df_merged` has `r fmt(nrow(df_merged))` rows for `r n_distinct(df_merged$iso3c)` countries, but only `r fmt(df_joins$both[df_joins$join == "full"])` rows for `r df_joins$countries[df_joins$join == "inner"]` countries have both values. Participation trends, GDP trends and the U-shape therefore use different samples, and the `r nrow(ilo_only)` ILO-only areas, mostly territories, never enter the U-shape. The panel is also unbalanced: the number of countries with both values rises from `r sum(df_merged$year == 1970 & !is.na(df_merged$flfp) & !is.na(df_merged$gdp_pc))` in 1970 to `r sum(df_merged$year == 2010 & !is.na(df_merged$flfp) & !is.na(df_merged$gdp_pc))` in 2010, so a change in an average can reflect which countries enter the data rather than change within countries.

### 3.3.5 - Are there any steps necessary in cleaning data after the merge? Pay attention to the missing values (if any) and explain how you deal with them.

Yes: we check the rows, make names and income groups consistent and handle the missing values.

```{r}
# Check : rows after the merge = ILO rows + World Bank rows - rows in both
nrow(df_merged)
nrow(df_ilo_merge) + nrow(df_wb_merge) - df_joins$rows[df_joins$join == "inner"]

# Check : still one row per country-year (0 = no duplicates)
df_merged |>
  count(iso3c, year) |>
  filter(n > 1) |>
  nrow()

# One income group per country (current World Bank group, the same every year)
df_income <- df_wb_clean |>
  distinct(iso3c, income)

# Check : number of countries with more than one group, and the groups used
df_income |>
  count(iso3c) |>
  filter(n > 1) |>
  nrow()
count(df_income, income)

# Name of every code from one source, income group as a factor in order
df_merged <- df_merged |>
  left_join(df_income, by = "iso3c") |>
  mutate(country = countrycode(iso3c, "iso3c", "country.name",
                               custom_match = custom_names),
         income  = factor(income, levels = c("Low income",
                                             "Lower middle income",
                                             "Upper middle income",
                                             "High income")))

# Check : rows unchanged, no missing name, no hidden missing value ("" or -99)
nrow(df_merged)
sum(is.na(df_merged$country))
sum(df_merged == "", na.rm = TRUE)
sum(df_merged == -99, na.rm = TRUE)
```

The row count matches, the key stays unique, names are complete and nothing is hidden as "" or -99. Each country has one current income group (four levels), used for every year; it is `NA` for the `r n_distinct(df_merged$iso3c[is.na(df_merged$income)])` areas without World Bank GDP.

```{r}
# Missing values per variable
colSums(is.na(df_merged))

# Rows with participation, GDP and both, by decade and by income group
df_merged |>
  mutate(decade = year %/% 10 * 10) |>
  group_by(decade) |>
  summarise(rows      = n(),
            with_flfp = sum(!is.na(flfp)),
            with_gdp  = sum(!is.na(gdp_pc)),
            both      = sum(!is.na(flfp) & !is.na(gdp_pc)))
df_merged |>
  group_by(income) |>
  summarise(countries = n_distinct(iso3c),
            rows      = n(),
            both      = sum(!is.na(flfp) & !is.na(gdp_pc)))

# Final order of columns and rows
df_merged <- df_merged |>
  select(iso3c, country, year, income, flfp, gdp_pc, log_gdp_pc) |>
  arrange(iso3c, year)

# Country-years with both values, for the U-shape in 3.5
df_both <- df_merged |>
  filter(!is.na(flfp), !is.na(gdp_pc))

# Overview of the final data
glimpse(df_merged)

# Save the merged data (R format)
saveRDS(df_merged, "data/df_merged.RDS")
```

`flfp` is missing in `r fmt(sum(is.na(df_merged$flfp)))` rows without an ILO estimate, `gdp_pc` in `r sum(is.na(df_merged$gdp_pc))` ILO rows without World Bank GDP (e.g. before `r min(df_wb_merge$year)`, territories). Complete rows are rarer in early decades and poorer countries, which suggests values are not missing completely at random: samples lean towards recent, richer country-years. We keep the `NA`s and do not impute, which would invent whole decades; each analysis uses and reports its complete cases. `df_merged` now has its seven final columns, and `df_both` `r fmt(nrow(df_both))` rows.

## 3.4 - Explore and visualize the data

As seen in 3.3.4, the countries in the data change over time, so a trend can reflect which countries enter the data. We therefore compare each trend with a balanced panel: the countries observed in every year of one common window.

```{r}
# Number of countries with a participation rate and with GDP, per year
coverage <- df_merged |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(n_flfp = sum(!is.na(flfp)),
            n_gdp  = sum(!is.na(gdp_pc)))

# Common window for both variables (chosen from the coverage above)
year_start <- 2000
year_end   <- 2022

# Countries with a participation rate in every year of the window
balanced_flfp <- df_merged |>
  filter(!is.na(flfp), year >= year_start, year <= year_end) |>
  count(iso3c) |>
  filter(n == year_end - year_start + 1)

# Countries with GDP per capita in every year of the window
balanced_gdp <- df_merged |>
  filter(!is.na(gdp_pc), year >= year_start, year <= year_end) |>
  count(iso3c) |>
  filter(n == year_end - year_start + 1)

# For comparison : balanced participation panel starting ten years earlier
balanced_flfp_early <- df_merged |>
  filter(!is.na(flfp), year >= year_start - 10, year <= year_end) |>
  count(iso3c) |>
  filter(n == year_end - year_start + 11)

# Number of countries in each panel
nrow(balanced_flfp)
nrow(balanced_gdp)
nrow(balanced_flfp_early)

# Income groups in the balanced participation panel
balanced_flfp_income <- df_merged |>
  filter(iso3c %in% balanced_flfp$iso3c, year == year_end) |>
  count(income)

balanced_flfp_income
```

We use `r year_start`–`r year_end`. Participation is sparse: a balanced panel starting ten years earlier would keep only `r nrow(balanced_flfp_early)` countries, and GDP coverage falls after `r year_end` (`r coverage$n_gdp[coverage$year == max(coverage$year)]` countries in `r max(coverage$year)` against `r coverage$n_gdp[coverage$year == year_end]`). The panels keep `r nrow(balanced_flfp)` countries for participation, `r balanced_flfp_income$n[balanced_flfp_income$income %in% "High income"]` of them high income, and `r nrow(balanced_gdp)` for GDP.

### 3.4.1 - Trends in female labour force participation

#### 3.4.1.1 - How did female labour force participation evolve over time? Interpret the trend exactly. What should we be aware of/careful when interpreting the trend?

```{r}
# Median participation per year : all countries and balanced panel
flfp_by_year <- bind_rows(
  "All countries" = df_merged |>
    filter(!is.na(flfp), year >= year_start, year <= year_end),
  "Balanced panel" = df_merged |>
    filter(!is.na(flfp), year >= year_start, year <= year_end,
           iso3c %in% balanced_flfp$iso3c),
  .id = "sample"
) |>
  group_by(sample, year) |>
  summarise(countries   = n(),
            median_flfp = median(flfp),
            .groups = "drop")

# Each line separately (used in the text)
flfp_all      <- flfp_by_year |> filter(sample == "All countries")
flfp_balanced <- flfp_by_year |> filter(sample == "Balanced panel")

ggplot(flfp_by_year, aes(x = year, y = median_flfp, color = sample)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Labour force participation of women aged 45-54",
       subtitle = paste("Median across countries. Balanced panel: the",
                        nrow(balanced_flfp), "countries observed every year"),
       x = "Year", y = "Participation rate (%)", color = "Sample",
       caption = "Source: ILOSTAT") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Participation rose steadily: in the balanced panel, the median went from `r round(flfp_balanced$median_flfp[1], 1)` % in `r year_start` to `r round(flfp_balanced$median_flfp[nrow(flfp_balanced)], 1)` % in `r year_end` (+`r round(flfp_balanced$median_flfp[nrow(flfp_balanced)] - flfp_balanced$median_flfp[1], 1)` percentage points), with only a small dip in 2020. We use the median because participation is left-skewed (3.2), and each country counts once, whatever its size. The all-countries line is lower and noisier (+`r round(flfp_all$median_flfp[nrow(flfp_all)] - flfp_all$median_flfp[1], 1)` points), because the `r min(flfp_all$countries)` to `r max(flfp_all$countries)` reporting countries change every year. The balanced panel is mostly high income, so its trend describes rich countries.

#### 3.4.1.2 - Is this trend similar for all countries? What is your hypothesis? Confirm or reject your hypothesis using your data.

Following Goldin, we expect participation to rise most in high-income countries and stagnate or fall in low-income countries, where it is already high (family farms). As the balanced panel has no low-income country, we compare country averages over the window's first and last ten years.

```{r}
# Average participation of each country in the first and last ten years
flfp_periods <- df_merged |>
  filter(!is.na(flfp), !is.na(income)) |>
  mutate(period = case_when(
    year >= year_start & year <= year_start + 9 ~ "first",
    year >= year_end - 9 & year <= year_end ~ "last"
  )) |>
  filter(!is.na(period)) |>
  group_by(iso3c, income, period) |>
  summarise(flfp = mean(flfp), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = period, values_from = flfp) |>
  filter(!is.na(first), !is.na(last))

# Median per income group (the change is computed country by country)
flfp_by_income <- flfp_periods |>
  group_by(income) |>
  summarise(countries    = n(),
            change       = median(last - first),
            median_first = median(first),
            median_last  = median(last))

# One point per period, placed at the middle year of the period
flfp_by_income |>
  pivot_longer(c(median_first, median_last),
               names_to = "period", values_to = "median_flfp") |>
  mutate(year = if_else(period == "median_first",
                        year_start + 4.5, year_end - 4.5)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = median_flfp, color = income)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Participation of women aged 45-54 by World Bank income group",
       subtitle = paste("Median of country averages over ", year_start, "-",
                        year_start + 9, " and ", year_end - 9, "-", year_end,
                        " (same ", nrow(flfp_periods), " countries)", sep = ""),
       x = "Middle year of the ten-year period",
       y = "Participation rate (%)",
       color = NULL, caption = "Source: ILOSTAT") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The data confirm the hypothesis: the median change rises with income, from `r round(flfp_by_income$change[1], 1)` points in low-income countries, which start highest (`r round(flfp_by_income$median_first[1], 1)` %), to +`r round(flfp_by_income$change[2], 1)`, +`r round(flfp_by_income$change[3], 1)` and +`r round(flfp_by_income$change[4], 1)` points in lower-middle, upper-middle and high-income countries. Groups are today's classification; the `r n_distinct(df_merged$iso3c[!is.na(df_merged$flfp) & is.na(df_merged$income) & df_merged$year >= year_start])` areas without one are excluded.

### 3.4.2 - Trends in GDP per capita

#### 3.4.2.1 - How did GDP per capita evolve over time? What should we be aware of/careful when interpreting the trend?

```{r}
# Median GDP per capita per year : all countries and balanced panel
gdp_by_year <- bind_rows(
  "All countries" = df_merged |>
    filter(!is.na(gdp_pc), year >= year_start, year <= year_end),
  "Balanced panel" = df_merged |>
    filter(!is.na(gdp_pc), year >= year_start, year <= year_end,
           iso3c %in% balanced_gdp$iso3c),
  .id = "sample"
) |>
  group_by(sample, year) |>
  summarise(countries  = n(),
            median_gdp = median(gdp_pc),
            .groups = "drop")

# Each line separately (used in the text)
gdp_all      <- gdp_by_year |> filter(sample == "All countries")
gdp_balanced <- gdp_by_year |> filter(sample == "Balanced panel")

ggplot(gdp_by_year, aes(x = year, y = median_gdp, color = sample)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "GDP per capita",
       subtitle = paste("Median across countries. Balanced panel: the",
                        nrow(balanced_gdp), "countries observed every year"),
       x = "Year", y = "GDP per capita (constant 2015 US$)", color = "Sample",
       caption = "Source: World Bank WDI") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

GDP per capita grew steadily: in the balanced panel, the median rose from `r fmt(round(gdp_balanced$median_gdp[1]))` US\$ in `r year_start` to `r fmt(round(gdp_balanced$median_gdp[nrow(gdp_balanced)]))` US\$ in `r year_end` (+`r round(100 * (gdp_balanced$median_gdp[nrow(gdp_balanced)] / gdp_balanced$median_gdp[1] - 1))` %), with a fall of `r round(100 * (1 - gdp_balanced$median_gdp[gdp_balanced$year == 2020] / gdp_balanced$median_gdp[gdp_balanced$year == 2019]), 1)` % in 2020. The all-countries line, with up to `r max(gdp_all$countries) - nrow(balanced_gdp)` more countries, ends `r fmt(round(gdp_all$median_gdp[nrow(gdp_all)] - gdp_balanced$median_gdp[nrow(gdp_balanced)]))` US\$ higher, so composition matters little. We use the unweighted median because GDP is right-skewed (3.2). Constant 2015 US\$ remove inflation but not price differences between countries (not PPP), and an average says nothing about inequality within a country.

#### 3.4.2.2 - Is this trend similar for rich and poor countries? Did the gap between them grow or shrink over time?

```{r}
# Median log GDP per capita per year and income group : balanced panel
gdp_by_income <- df_merged |>
  filter(iso3c %in% balanced_gdp$iso3c, year >= year_start, year <= year_end) |>
  group_by(income, year) |>
  summarise(median_log_gdp = median(log_gdp_pc), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(gdp_by_income, aes(x = year, y = median_log_gdp, color = income)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "GDP per capita by World Bank income group",
       subtitle = paste("Median across the", nrow(balanced_gdp),
                        "countries of the balanced panel"),
       x = "Year", y = "Log of GDP per capita (constant 2015 US$)",
       color = NULL, caption = "Source: World Bank WDI") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
# Robustness : rich and poor defined by GDP in year_start (top/bottom quarter)
gdp_start <- df_merged |>
  filter(iso3c %in% balanced_gdp$iso3c, year == year_start)
quarters <- quantile(gdp_start$gdp_pc, c(0.25, 0.75))

groups_start <- gdp_start |>
  mutate(rich_poor = case_when(gdp_pc <= quarters[1] ~ "poor",
                               gdp_pc >= quarters[2] ~ "rich")) |>
  filter(!is.na(rich_poor)) |>
  select(iso3c, rich_poor)

# Median GDP of the rich and poor groups, gap in US$ and ratio
gdp_gap <- bind_rows(
  "Income group (World Bank, today)" = df_merged |>
    filter(iso3c %in% balanced_gdp$iso3c,
           income %in% c("Low income", "High income")) |>
    mutate(rich_poor = if_else(income == "High income", "rich", "poor")),
  "Quarter of GDP in first year" = df_merged |>
    inner_join(groups_start, by = "iso3c"),
  .id = "definition"
) |>
  filter(year %in% c(year_start, year_end)) |>
  group_by(definition, year, rich_poor) |>
  summarise(median_gdp = median(gdp_pc), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = rich_poor, values_from = median_gdp) |>
  mutate(difference = rich - poor,
         ratio      = rich / poor)

# Each definition separately, first year then last year (used in the text)
gap_wb       <- gdp_gap |> filter(definition != "Quarter of GDP in first year")
gap_quarters <- gdp_gap |> filter(definition == "Quarter of GDP in first year")

gdp_gap |>
  mutate(poor       = fmt(round(poor)),
         rich       = fmt(round(rich)),
         difference = fmt(round(difference)),
         ratio      = round(ratio, 1)) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Rich and poor defined by", "Year",
                             "Poor (US\\$)", "Rich (US\\$)",
                             "Difference (US\\$)", "Ratio rich / poor"))
```

The trend is similar in direction but not in speed: all groups grew, the poorest fastest (+`r round(100 * (gap_wb$poor[2] / gap_wb$poor[1] - 1))` % for the median low-income country against +`r round(100 * (gap_wb$rich[2] / gap_wb$rich[1] - 1))` % for high income). On a log axis the vertical distance between two lines is a ratio, so the narrowing distance between the low- and high-income lines means a shrinking relative gap. The ratio fell from `r format(round(gap_wb$ratio[1], 1), nsmall = 1)` to `r format(round(gap_wb$ratio[2], 1), nsmall = 1)`, but the absolute gap grew from `r fmt(round(gap_wb$difference[1]))` to `r fmt(round(gap_wb$difference[2]))` US\$, since a faster growth rate on a much lower income adds fewer dollars. Today's groups partly sort countries by later growth, so we also define rich and poor as the top and bottom quarter of GDP in `r year_start` (`r sum(groups_start$rich_poor == "rich")` countries each): the ratio still falls, from `r format(round(gap_quarters$ratio[1], 1), nsmall = 1)` to `r format(round(gap_quarters$ratio[2], 1), nsmall = 1)`. These are unweighted medians on a balanced panel, so composition does not drive the result.
